newsitem.title: USA: Mafia turncoat says he will fight book lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Mafia turncoat says he will fight book lawsuit.

text.p: Former New York mobster Salvatore Gravano said on Friday he would fight attempts by relatives of his murder victims to recover money he made from a best-selling memoir on his life in the Mafia.

On the second day of Gravano's testimony in the murder and racketeering trial of reputed Genovese crime family boss Vincent "The Chin" Gigante, the defence tried to portray Gravano as a liar motivated by greed.

Under New York law, Gravano is not allowed to make money from an account of his crimes, which included 19 murders. He testified on Thursday that he was paid $250,000, expected royalties and wanted one million dollars from any movie deal.
The book's author, Peter Maas, and publisher HarperCollins denied they had paid Gravano any money.

The 52-year-old former Gambino crime family underboss, also known as "Sammy the Bull", was arrested in 1990 and opted to cooperate with the government rather than face life in prison. He has been in hiding since.
Gravano has evaded attempts by lawyers for the families of some of his murder victims to subpoena him in a civil lawsuit to recover money he made from "Underboss", the book published in April.
"I intend to fight that law and those cases," Gravano said under cross-examination from Gigante's attorney Michael Marinaccio in Brooklyn Federal Court.
Gravano's testimony helped convict reputed Godfather John Gotti in 1992.
Hammering away at Gravano's ability to tell the truth, the defence attorney recalled advice Gravano gave his former mob partners on evading and lying in court.
Marinaccio quoted Gravano as having said the mob was "all lies, all bullshit, it's one doublecross after another, one scheme after another and one betrayal after another."

On Thursday, Gravano identified Gigante as the head of the Genovese crime family. Gigante faces a 21-count murder and racketeering indictment. His attorneys say he has been incapacitated by mental illness for years, but prosecutors say he has feigned illness to avoid prosecution.
Turning again to Gravano's best-selling book, Gigante's lawyer got Gravano to admit he had no basis to judge Gigante's sanity.

In the book, Gravano is quoted as saying about Gigante: "Maybe he enjoyed driving the feds nuts, which he was." In another line, he seems to contradict himelf saying "sometimes I would think he was crazy, and then take medication when he had to be sane."
Gigante is accused of ordering the killing of seven people and conspiring to kill three others, allegedly to avenge breaches of Mafia protocol such as unauthorised slayings.
